A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodeClash, with readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Retained material can be matched reliably, including relocated displays and the new appendices D.5–D.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original model tournaments, leaderboard results, behavioral analyses, ablations, and Claude Sonnet 4.5's evaluation against a human-written RobotRumble bot.

after.justification: v2 retains the original tournament results and adds human-solution ladder evaluations, human annotation agreement measurements, and a scaffold comparison.

M1.justification: v2 adds CC:Ladder as a procedural variant: initialize from the weakest human solution, advance conditionally through ranked opponents, and retain the codebase between opponents. The underlying models, editing mechanism, and two-phase CodeClash loop remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The human evaluation expands from one expert RobotRumble opponent to human-solution ladders in RobotRumble and Core War. Besides broader human-opponent coverage, the ladder introduces sustained progression across opponents. The original six-arena model evaluation remains unchanged.

E2.justification: The gigachad-only human comparison is replaced by ranked human-solution pools, with GPT-5, GPT-5 mini, and Gemini 2.5 Pro joining Claude Sonnet 4.5 in that evaluation. Table 7 newly evaluates SWE-agent against mini-SWE-agent. The original eight-model leaderboard membership is retained.

E3.justification: The human evaluation changes from fixed 15-round tournaments against one bot to seven-round ladder stages, human-solution initialization, conditional advancement, and highest-defeated-rank scoring. D.5 adds stratified sampling of 100 trajectories and binary human annotations. The ladder threshold is inconsistent: Section 4.1 requires a majority, but D.6.2's > floor(n/3) permits three wins out of seven.

E4.justification: New Appendix D.5 checks the automated trajectory judgments against three human annotators. D.6.4 adds a scaffold ablation across three models and two arenas. These address previously untested annotation reliability and scaffold sensitivity; existing transparency, multiplayer, and behavioral analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces inter-human Fleiss' kappa, human–GPT-5 Cohen's kappa, and agreement percentages. It also specifies best-of-five ladder reporting and best-of-three scaffold-ablation reporting, without reporting ladder dispersion. The existing Elo uncertainty calculations and 1,000-replicate bootstrap analyses are unchanged.

E6.justification: The detailed gigachad results—zero wins in 150 rounds and 37,500 simulations—are replaced by ladder results, led by GPT-5 mini at 57/58 in RobotRumble and 260/264 in Core War. New results include 91%, 88%, and 94% human–judge agreement and scaffold differences of zero to two ranks. Main leaderboard values remain unchanged; the human evaluations use different settings.

T1.justification: D.6 introduces a mathematically specified ladder advancement condition and defines the score as the highest opponent rank defeated. Its threshold conflicts with the majority description. The existing Bradley–Terry likelihood, Elo conversion, covariance derivation, and bootstrap formulation remain unchanged; no new proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and concluding takeaway retain the same benchmark contribution and principal claims about diverse solutions, strategic weaknesses, poor codebase maintenance, and the human-expert gap. The zero-win expert claim remains, although its detailed supporting experiment is removed.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the single-bot qualification and scaffold-as-future-work discussion with broader robustness arguments about scaffolds, budgets, and prompting. It newly interprets ladder termination as failure to consolidate gains and human agreement as validating the automated judge. D.5 also adds an interpretation of hallucination disagreements.

D1.justification: D.5–D.6 document annotation sampling, human-solution collection, 250/4,000 simulations per human matchup, and L2 regularization strength 0.01. They add repository access instructions for annotations, agreement scripts, ranked solutions, and ladder evaluation. Existing infrastructure and prompt documentation largely remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Landis and Koch (1977) to support interpretation of annotation agreement. The related-work coverage and principal positioning against coding, optimization, game-playing, and self-improvement research remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds two authors and an affiliation, makes localized wording corrections, rewrites the human-comparison passage and discussion, and appends D.5–D.6. The overall section organization and most explanatory prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 2, 6, and 7 and removes v1's Figure 47 leaderboard screenshot. Subsequent figures are renumbered or relocated, with limited caption and page-flow changes. Most original figures and tables retain their displays.

improvement.justification: Human validation of the automated judge and broader human/scaffold evaluations provide useful evidence absent from v1. However, the ladder advancement rule is internally inconsistent, Tables 1–2 do not substantiate the claimed ranking consistency, and the detailed zero-win experiment is removed while its headline claim remains. These problems affect reproducibility and interpretation of an important addition. The benefits and harms do not establish a reliable net quality improvement.
